utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, December 11, 2008, and I welcome all representatives of the OTP, Ms. Dahl, Ms. Biersay, their case manager. I welcome our witness, and I greet Mr. Seselj and everyone helping us. Mr. Seselj is about to continue with his -- is about to start with his cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I meant to do that at the end - I assume we'll have time - but I want to start my cross-examination straight away, if I may, if you have nothing against it. I can of course do it now, but I'd prefer to do it later. If you insist, I'll do it straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed with your cross-examination, and then we will deal with pending questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, when you decided to be a Defence witness, you gave several statements to my legal advisers; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In one of those statements, you set out, in detail, the first pressure exerted upon you to give false testimony against me, and that was pressure exerted by Zoran Djindjic; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You described how a man called you up on the phone and said he was somebody from his offices, a man called Markovic, and conveyed the message that Djindjic wished to talk to you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, you have that statement attached to my submission three months ago, when I asked for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If we could have the date of that statement, perhaps it would assist us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, certainly. It's the statement of the 11th of August, 2008. You have it in that set of statements that I attached to my submission with the request that Defence witnesses be protected, and that's been translated into English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said there that you were surprised, firstly, and then that you agreed to talk, and then that this meeting was scheduled for -- or, rather, somewhere in Kosutnjak; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in the Kosutnjak forest. Well, that's not where the talk was supposed to take place, but it was said that I should come to the Federal Assembly in Belgrade and then go to Zoran Djindjic and have a talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this Kosutnjak area, what facility was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there is no facility. It's just a park.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were outside in the park?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That's a nice part of Kosutnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You knew Zoran Djindjic from before?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I never met him, but I knew him as a public personage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You would see him in the Assembly, in the Assembly halls, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he greeted you there as if you were an old friend?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, because I don't want to ask a leading question so as to make what I have to say more convincing, what did Zoran Djindjic say to you straight away, when he saw you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Zoran Djindjic said that we should stabilise the new government, that it was a government supported by the West, and that the West was ready to invest a large amount of money into Serbia, and that that was the only way out for Serbia, but that the strengthening of power in Serbia had an obstacle, a serious obstacle, and that was Dr. Vojislav Seselj and the Serbian Radical Party, and that we should suppress Dr. Vojislav Seselj and that we should marginalise the Serbian Radical Party. And once that is achieved, then the government and powers in Serbia will be stable. And he also said, just like all the rest of them, that Dr. Vojislav Seselj was far more dangerous than Slobodan Milosevic, and the Serbian Radical Party was more dangerous for pro-Western policy than the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he was quite right in saying that, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he was right, inasmuch as you, as a politician, as a leader, were more consistent in waging your policies and politics on the basis of a party programme, on the basis of your visions, on the basis of your ideology and convictions, and on the basis of the fact that you entered politics to do something for your own people and not to pilfer the country, as the other structures in power were doing from Djindjic to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the West doesn't like the pro-Russian policies of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he also say that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did you tell him? He knew that you were in conflict with me and the Serbian Radical Party and had been for a number of years?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he wanted to use that and to use me to keep you at arm's length, you and the Serbian Radical Party. Now, he suggested various things to me, and in return he would provide a good life for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did any possible war crimes on my part or on the part of the volunteers of the Serbian Party, were they ever mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not specifically. No specific crimes were mentioned, or events. It was more in general terms that it was the policy and politics waged by Dr. Seselj, his ideology, that it was in fact a war ideology, and that that kind of ideology and the policies waged by you were an obstacle to the West, and that that kind of politics and ideology should be suppressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that he had some firm arguments to disqualify me and the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, no, he didn't, in my opinion, have any firm arguments. All that was needed -- or, rather, he needed people who would serve his purpose, the purpose of some invented, fabricated policy with some nonexistent proof, false proof and evidence. That's how I understood his intentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that one had to morally disqualify me by inventing things and presenting fabrications?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not the first time that the regime in Serbia tried to discredit me in that way; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the Slobodan Milosevic regime did that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On several occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you tell Djindjic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told him that I couldn't act against my convictions, I was -- that I didn't agree with everything Dr. Seselj was doing or the Serbian Radical Party, but that I could not take part in a campaign of that kind and conduct of that kind. That was unacceptable, as far as I was concerned. I didn't enter politics to be a politician at all cost. I entered politics on the basis of my convictions and on the basis of my deep psychological and moral need to help my own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what was Djindjic's reaction to that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Djindjic reacted fairly violently. He said, "What patriotism, what convictions? We have to work for the state. Leave all that behind. You should see how you're to survive, how you're going to live. I know that you have a very modest pension and that you deserve more and can do more." And then he asked that I call him again in a week's time to arrange our cooperation and see how we were going to cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you call him up ten days later?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I considered Djindjic, although he is dead now, I think he's a criminal hooligan and I think he's somebody without any credibility whatsoever and not capable of heading the government of a state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened afterwards, when you refused to call him up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, then on the 7th of May they took me into the headquarters of the special police or people from the State Security, as they introduced themselves. They interrogated me without stop for 20 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did they insist upon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they insisted upon the fact that I had received a bribe of some kind. They showed me a disc of some sort, a CD, in which I gave my associates, among deputies, me providing documents for the pre-electoral campaign and activities, and me giving them some money, some of the party money. Now, that was the time before the elections, just before the elections, because they were held in September, and this all happened -- my meeting, that is, with my associates took place sometime at the end of July. What we wanted to do was to prepare in advance for the elections and on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, did they make ultimatums and say that if you didn't agree to cooperate against me, that you would be taken to court and legal proceedings taken against you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, not everybody, but, yes, they did, a number of them did. And I think one of them was the main person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One of those agents, did they tell your wife something on that occasion when they ransacked or searched your flat?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That agent, at the time when they were waiting to take me into the police station on the first day, on the 7th, I think, that was the day after my patron saint's day, family patron saint's day, I was not in my flat. They entered the flat, the three of them, and one of them -- well, later on we learned that that was the Chef de Cabinet of the chief of State Security of Serbia, and he said that they had been directly sent -- they were there on orders, direct orders from Zoran Djindjic to take me into custody. And they said the same thing from the State Security, those people said the same thing in Pancevo, the State Security in Pancevo, who two days later searched my mother-in-law's flat in Pancevo, and they also said that that was something directly demanded by Zoran Djindjic, and that he was -- they were told that by the head of the State Security Department for Pancevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, could you, just for the record, tell us which date did you receive the first call from Mr. Djindjic, and when did you subsequently meet up with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, Your Honour, that was in mid-April. I don't remember the exact date, but I do know that it was sometime around midday, around noon, and that this man, Mr. Markovic, said he'd call me that day and that he'd tell me when Mr. Djindjic would receive me. But he didn't call up that day; he called the following day at 11.00, and then we arranged to meet in the afternoon, at around 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yeah, 2001, when he came into power, immediately, this new government that overthrew Slobodan Milosevic and his government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Djindjic's government, as far as I remember, was formed in January 2001. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The elections were at the end of December 2000?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then Zoran Djindjic became the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And that's when the fierce clashes began straight away between the ruling coalition and the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct. They undermined or, rather, abused the consistency of the Serbian Radical Party, who in following the electoral results to the very end, informed the public very correctly on the results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the time, it was -- in Parliament, they prevented us from taking the floor and stating our views from the rostrum, and that they threw us out of the Assembly, they made us pay fines, the police hustled us out, and all that was in this campaign to keep the Serbian Radical Party quiet?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I understood it that they had come into power, but that they had seen that there were a lot of problems facing them in setting up government and successfully leading the state, and then they wanted to marginalise and silence the only party that had a strong voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the leading people in Djindjic's regime accused me publicly that I engaged in crime and abused my position as the vice-premier and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they manage to find a single shred of evidence for that serious allegation of theirs?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, they didn't, and they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was just one criminal report filed against me at that time, a single one, a criminal report, because as vice-premier, I signed a government decision that part of the money from the fund for assistance to earthquake-stricken areas should be rechanneled to those suffering from floods, because in the summer of 1999 we had a lot of floods in Central Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then they gave up on that criminal report and having proceedings taken further?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know that nothing -- it wasn't taken up afterwards. Nothing actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But there were many other criminals reports filed against me and procedure taken for slander, because they said I had attacked ministers, Prime Ministers accused of being involved in various affairs and so on and so forth; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because from the very beginning when the authority and the new government was set up in Serbia, I knew that they were people of doubtful -- well, we didn't know where their riches came from, and recently a paper in Serbia wrote about the disillusionment of the head of the American CIA in the protagonists of the new government in Serbia. In fact he was criticising with his associates who had brought into power in Serbia just pure criminals and people who were incapable and thereby compromised the policies and politics of the West.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly be asked to slow down and speak one at a time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Congress in America published public information that in 2000, in toppling Milosevic, they invested $150 million, the Americans?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are speaking too fast, and the interpreters are having a difficult time keeping track with you. Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember, Mr. Seselj, that that had been discussed, but I forgot the figure. But as for now, there is this one figure in relation to your position as president of the Serb Radical Party. That's one that I know for sure; namely, the Americans, through their intelligence services, provided $100 million to Tomislav Nikolic and Vucic, and the tycoons of Serbia gave the rest in order for the figure to be 300 million Euro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Quite frankly, I have to tell you that the figure seems to be a fantastic one to me.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not fantastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not prone to believe it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Witness, but when did this happen, what you say allegedly happened with the Americans? When did it happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to Tomislav Nikolic, that happened this year, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it's not relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then I will give decided questions [as interpreted] to Mr. Seselj's questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that from 1990 onwards, the Americans were financing the pro-Western opposition in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do know that, because for the most part it was Vuk Draskovic who took part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Democratic Party; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the Democratic Party, but just one wing. I mean, the part of the party that consisted of Kosta Cavoski, Marko Jankovic and Vojislav Kostunica and others did not take part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Soon they left the Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did, just like many socialists left who had been founding members of that party, people of integrity, of convictions, who were in favour of a modern socialist party, of a pro-European profile. All of them left the Socialist Party, and it was mostly criminals who took over that party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now came May 2003, and you were called in to the Belgrade office of The Hague Tribunal; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it was 2004. But if you're saying "2003" --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On your alleged statement, it says 2003.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, I think it was 2004, but it doesn't really change things, it doesn't change the essence. First from The Hague, some Philip Petrovic called me, and he connected me with someone from the OTP, I no longer remember the name. And then that person said to me with -- through the interpretation of Mr. Petrovic, that I had to enter a cooperation with the representatives of the OTP in Belgrade and that I should make a statement. And when I asked in what capacity should I make a statement, as an accused person or a witness, they said, "It doesn't matter, but you have to cooperate." That happened on the 4th of May, just before my patron saint's day. And about ten days later, I don't know exactly how many days later, a person called me from The Hague Tribunal, I mean Paolo Stocchi. Again, of course, he spoke through an interpreter, and he said that I had to come to the offices of The Hague Tribunal in Dedinje. I went on the day that was agreed upon, and I spent four days there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, here in the statements, it says that there were two persons who took part in this meeting, Philippe Oberknezev and Paolo Pastore-Stocchi?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what the name of the other person is. He just said that he was a Frenchman of Russian origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Philippe Oberknezev speak Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Well, he didn't show any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He didn't show that he was of Serb origin? He claimed that he was of Russian origin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said that he was a Frenchman of Russian origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you hear of Milos Oberknezevic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me remind you. You are an educated person. When Pavelic looked at the remaining Serb -- Orthodox Serbs in the so-called independent state of Croatia, when he wanted to set up an Orthodox Church, he appointed a Russian emigre as the patriarch and Milos Oberknezevic was the number two man of that church. He was a metropolitan priest. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that activity of the Ante Pavelic and the Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Right. So I have no proof that this Philippe Oberknezev is related to Milos Oberknezevic, but since this is a very rare surname, it's symptomatic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since it's symptomatic, let us leave it aside for the time being. Right. Now, this interview that went on for four days, how long did it go on during the course of one day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: From 9.00 until 5.00 or 6.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Eight or nine hours a day?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, it was a bit shorter, but it was regular working hours and even longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: More than 30 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And after these exhausting interviews, you could hardly wait for them to be over?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, because Paolo Stocchi made it seem that I would be interrogated even further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's when you signed what they gave you to sign in English; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And yesterday you said that they never read it out to you in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: They didn't, and I didn't ask for it either. I just wanted for it all to be over as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: claims that she read it back to you in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember that her name was Dana.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what really matters to me is she did not read it back to you, and what her name was doesn't matter at all. All right. Now, tell me, please, during that conversation, both Stocchi and Oberknezev for the most part insisted on my moral disqualification; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right. I quickly convinced them that I did not know about any war crimes, that I was not at the front-line, that I did not participate in the war, and that I really did not know about any kind of war crimes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are at this time requesting that the name of the interpreter be redacted. I understand that it's considered sensitive in Belgrade, so I've been informed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is not a sensitive issue at all in Belgrade, and there is no reason to redact it. No official of The Hague Tribunal in Belgrade ever had any kind of personal problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After deliberating, the Trial Chamber decides to redact the name. It's irrelevant, anyway. It's irrelevant when it comes to the issue. And so at line 20, please, line 24, page 14, please redact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what the problem is there, Judges? You redact one name, and indeed that name is deleted from the transcript. That's no problem. However, on the recording, the Registry deletes an entire passage. From the video clip, the Registry does not redact only that name but an entire section of the hearings, and then the public is denied the opportunity to view the entire proceedings. And that is why I complain this much about redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, as far as redaction is concerned, I sign an order and the name is deleted. All the rest remains. You're saying that there is more that is deleted than just the name, but I'll check, because normally the name is deleted and all the rest stays unchanged. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I see here is that they tried to carry this slander out in two different ways; by providing information that I had lots of money and that I got it in an illegal way, and, secondly, that I was linked to various killings. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned that in 1992 and in 1993, we had a certain number of sponsors, but I hope that you will agree with me that, for the most part, these were small-scale sponsors.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was that truck of fuel that was the biggest piece of sponsorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that in 1992 and 1993, Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were under an embargo?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was no gasoline at the gasoline stations?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that we had to make do in order to get each and every jerry can of gasoline in order to be able to travel through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mentioned this company that was headed by Petar Vujasinovic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was surprised here when you said that he was involved in export and import.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: [No translation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, a significant passage is missing. It was too fast for interpretation and for the court reporter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. You're too fast. The court reporter can't follow, can't keep track. Therefore, he stops everything. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to slow down, but time is always somehow too short for me, and I want to achieve as much as possible within a single hour. So I don't even feel it, but I really speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, you said yesterday that Stocchi insisted that I had property that was valued at $50 million US?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he insisted on that, but I found that to be fantastic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, now, let's see, where could this property possibly be? If it is immovable property, it cannot be hidden at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You cannot hide real estate and that kind of big money?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's look at bank accounts now. Can it be hidden in any way?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. As a person accused in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Every bank transaction can easily be traced?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thirdly, if it is in cash, you know that what is in circulation now are bank notes of $100?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There are no bigger bank notes in circulation. A few decades ago, the Americans printed bills of 1.000, 5.000, 10.000, but then they were quickly withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So it would mean 500.000 bills of $100?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's a truckload, then? If it were all to be tied up in bundles, that would be 5.000 bundles; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, for these 5.000 bundles to be loaded into these regular briefcases, you'd need 50 briefcases, because one can take about 10?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your math is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't really need a truck, but you would need one of those small trucks or vans to carry that around. So this is something that sounds truly fantastic, and nevertheless they insisted that this be included in your statement. Why?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they wanted to get me involved in this against you in every conceivable way, to show that you were a person who was prone to crime, that you were a violent person, a person who is not fit to be in politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see, it also says here that my wife, Jadranka Seselj, owns an export/import company. Do you know that when my wife, Jadranka, married me, she was immediately laid off, dismissed, from the company where she had worked until then?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really don't know about your lady wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If she really had a company, somebody would have known about this, they'd have a document?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, all the opposition parties would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, only perhaps it would be possible if my wife was engaged in some kind of business on the side, without me knowing it, and now Paolo Stocchi is helping me do that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think your wife is an honourable person and she really wouldn't do anything without you knowing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Hague Tribunal would want me to be suspicious of my wife and to ask for part of the profits of this company.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Hague OTP or, rather, someone from the OTP is looking at all possible ways and means of presenting you as a bad person who is working against the interests of the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, these accusations that I was involved in killings, first of all, this was the -- it was the Democratic Party that said that I killed Vojin Vuletic, and then Slobodan Jovic, and that I killed him wife Paska, and now I cannot even remember who it was that said that I killed Oliver Dennis, a Chetnik vojvoda, who I held in high esteem, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that Vojin Vuletic was a very sick man and that that was the cause of his death, illness. I even socialised with him. As for Paska Jovic, that story was launched and kept on the burner, as it were, by his wife -- by her husband, Slobodan Jovic. He exerted such pressure against all of us that he came across. He wanted us to believe his assertion that Mr. Seselj had something to do with this. At that time, I was head of the Deputies Club that cooperated with the Socialist Party or, rather, the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I took Slobodan Jovic to the then Minister of the Interior of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Vukasin Jokanovic, so that he would say to Slobodan Jovic what the police knew about that case. Vukasin Jokanovic, at the meeting at his office, and I think this was in 1995, stated explicitly that Vojislav Seselj and the Serb Radical Party had nothing to do with this whatsoever. However, even that was not sufficient for Slobodan Jovic. We went together to the then Minister of the Interior of Serbia, Zoran Sokolovic. Zoran Sokolovic gave us the names of three men who were then under investigation for the killing of Paska Jovic. Of course, later on it was publicly disclosed that this was one man, a man who was a criminal and a pervert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when such lies are launched in the public, did anyone serious in the Serbian public opinion believe this or did they just thing that this was something that was tabloid fodder?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, serious people didn't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After that, did the rating of the Serb Radical Party just go up?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly, because the logical conclusion was, in relation to such nebulous accusations, that this was a dirt campaign against Vojislav Seselj and the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a very short follow-up question. Mr. Seselj puts a series of questions about a series of crimes. I suppose that there were investigations into those crimes in your country. I know and we know that there are high-quality investigative judges working in your country, and they must have carried out investigations into those crimes. As far as you know, the offenders, were they identified, tried? Were they convicted, as far as you know? In all these cases, did Serbian justice at any time incriminate Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An investigation was carried out. I knew that, and sentences were passed out to the perpetrators. But the name of Dr. Vojislav Seselj never appeared in the investigation or during the trial. Well, the police and the law found out the suspects and through an investigation and legal proceedings and trials and a judgement which was passed, the perpetrators were found and they were sentenced, and in both -- in these cases that Mr. Seselj mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember how we, the Serb Radicals, in the second half of 1993, clashed with Slobodan Milosevic and the Socialist Party, and how this fierce clash went on right up until the end of 1997?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well. I took part in it. Slobodan Milosevic, using television and other information media, ascribed various things to you, or rather the Slobodan Milosevic regime did, and all the protagonists of the system of the day, his propaganda and so on, they ascribed it to you and blamed you for engaging in violence and many other negative things, and they made it impossible for you and the Serbian Radical Party to respond to the accusations made against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anybody ever use more brutal words to attack Slobodan Milosevic and his wife, Mira Markovic, than me? Did anybody use worse words than me?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nobody dared think along those lines, let alone utter the kind of things that you uttered. And I remember some of your accusations, the ones that you hurled against them. I remember them today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they're to be found in the titles of my books as well, right, because with my book titles, I showed what I thought about the people who wielded might and were at the head of the government?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. You were -- you never compromised in unveiling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me this: Could -- had Milosevic's regime been able to find anything that compromised me, would they have used it to finally settle accounts with me?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he would use anything that he could find, because he treated you as the most -- his most serious political adversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They arrested me three times and threw me into prison, first of all because of an incident in the Federal Assembly. The second time was because of an incident in the Federal Assembly again, and the third time, because I held a banned rally in Gnjilane; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in this period from 1993 to 1997, I was in prison three times exclusively for politics, for reasons of politics?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was never any crime involved, was there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, the next time the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, in September 2006, asked you to come to their premises; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they did ask me to do that, but I didn't want to go. And then Paolo Stocchi said that one of the OTP representatives would come to see me anywhere I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that Daniel Saxon?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And a woman with him?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a lady who introduced herself and said she was from New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then in your own flat, according to your statement, and that's your statement of the 19th of November, 2007, for the Prosecutor to be able to follow, in your own words, he insisted that Dr. Seselj should be depicted in The Hague Tribunal in such a way that he be politically eliminated, and he said that you could help them there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You say he insisted upon that when he saw that he could learn nothing from me about war crime allegations?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he put the same ideas forward as the late Zoran Djindjic. He also said that the new government should be stabilised, that the only way out for Serbia was a pro-Western government, that all those against that government should be suppressed, and the most serious adversary to Western policy was Dr. Vojislav Seselj and the Serbian Radical Party, so he should be rendered impotent. And I had the impression that Dan Saxon was far more oriented towards implementing politics and the activities of the US CIA than his legal functions and court functions. He acknowledged that he was an official of certain American structures and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Yes, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I understand that this witness has some training as a lawyer. I would request that the Court remind him about the possibility of perjury charges being brought and under what conditions that could happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are a lawyer. You must keep this in mind. You are testifying under oath. You made a solemn declaration. You are aware of the scope of such a declaration. Now you describe a meeting with an OTP investigator [as interpreted] and with an investigator, and you allege that this man said that Mr. Seselj has to be put out of the political loop, as it were. Is this something that you're saying under oath? We agree on that? This is being said under oath, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under oath, and the oath makes it incumbent upon me to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, equally, you do confirm, Witness, that you signed, with your own hand, a statement given to Saxon, Stocchi, a statement in which you were saying just the opposite? So can you confirm that you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, forgive me for interrupting, but just to clarify, the statement, which is 65 ter number, I believe, 7427, was signed in 2003. That is the only statement that was ever signed for the OTP by this witness. With respect to that statement, Mr. Saxon did not in any way participate in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Biersay. So you signed a statement given to the investigator, to Paolo Stocchi, and you signed it, confirming what was written in it. You equally signed a statement in which the interpreter certified that your entire statement had been read back to you in Serbian; everything had been translated from English into Serbian. And you did sign. We have it in front of us. Can you confirm that you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did sign, but I told you what pressure I was under. It was not translated to me or interpreted to me, and the statement is in English and I don't understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you did sign that this statement was translated back to you into Serbian. So did you sign a fake document? Are you confirming this here in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't translated back to me. I stand by that, and that's the truth of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, even if this statement had been read out to you in Serbian, you had absolutely no possibility of checking to see whether the interpreter read it out to you in full?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were left to the will of the translator and interpreter to make restrictions, change the contents of the statement, or do anything that he had been given orders to do?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers speak one at a time, please. We did not catch the answer. It was overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was written by the interpreter, so that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it's your impression that the interview would have gone on for five or six days, had you not signed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin and Mr. Seselj, again you're overlapping, making it impossible for the Judges to understand the conversation between you. You are both lawyers, and you both know how these things work. You should be able to do better, so please observe a pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do take this into account. What was said by my fellow Judge is very important indeed. Let me get back to this essential thing. You are testifying under oath, so we take it for granted that what you're saying is true, unless there is perjury. I have your statement signed in English, of course. The statement in your own language is not signed. At any rate, I don't have it. It is a statement of exactly 19 pages, the 20th page, being the last one, in which you stated that the 20 pages were read back to you in your own language. If 20 pages were read back to you in your language, it takes at least an hour for the 20 pages to be read back to you in your own language slowly for you to understand. The question is very simple. I'm not going to name the interpreter, but did the interpreter read the 20 pages, starting with the very first word saying: "My name is Jovan Glamocanin. I am a Serb male ...," et cetera? Did she read the 20 pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your answer, she didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Therefore, were you given the document in English, did you sign it, did you initial it, just in your stride?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber feels it is necessary, there is one very simple solution to this problem. We just need to hear the interpreter. Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Excuse me, Mr. Seselj. Just for the record, Your Honour, we would move that the statement, which has been the subject of much discussion, be given at least an MFI number, and that would be 65 ter number 7427.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's give an MFI number to the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement shall be given Exhibit number P688, marked for identification. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, you're a lawyer, you have many years of experience -- or, rather, a legal man. In the Serbian legal system, can any statement be valid which a citizen signed and it is written in a language he doesn't understand at all?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it cannot be valid. It must be in a language which the person signing understands and knows well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You described here how, on the 16th of September, 2006, Ms. Christine Dahl came to your flat with Paolo Stocchi, an interpreter and two policemen?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, that was on the 15th of November, 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 2007, you say?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you go on to explain that while you were talking to them, one of the policemen went to your daughter's room, sat down at the computer, and checked to see what was on the hard disc there; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Paolo Stocchi even mentioned that your daughter used the internet at night too much; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And from that, you draw the conclusion that you were being -- you were under surveillance from The Hague investigators or the Serb police that provided them with intelligence about you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes. By stating that, Mr. Stocchi said it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he said that you would be arrested and forcibly taken to The Hague if you failed to sign?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stocchi and Ms. Dahl mentioned all the measures they could take and steps they could take and resources they had to force me to come in and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 27th of February --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. Witness, now you are incriminating the investigator from the OTP. You said that he went to check the computer, to check the hard disc in the computer. This is a serious allegation. You know that, technically, that can be ascertained. Why did you not think of asking the lawyer to start proceedings for an independent expert to check the hard disc in order to show that at a precise time, one file was opened or there was one search launched? Didn't that occur to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It didn't occur to me. As for my daughter's computer, it was a Serb policeman that was handling it, not Mr. Stocchi. Mr. Stocchi just said that our daughter uses the internet for a long time during the night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was the Serbian policeman who was there who started the computer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Serb policeman came with a team that was headed by Ms. Dahl, and first he came into the apartment on his own, and he said that he first had to search the apartment and that it was only then that Ms. Dahl and the rest could come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're a distinguished lawyer, so what was the legal authority allowing a Serbian policeman first to get into your apartment and, secondly, to access a computer? Is there any legal foundation in that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I know that in order to have a search carried out, a policeman has to have a warrant, a search warrant. However, I did not want to refuse to talk to Ms. Dahl, because she's a Prosecutor, she came all the way from The Hague. Of course, it wasn't only for the sake of talking to me that she came, but I did accept to talk to her in my apartment and I did not want to refuse to have Ms. Dahl and Mr. Stocchi come, since they had arrived in front of the apartment building where my apartment is. Therefore, although there was this deficiency in terms of the procedure involved and the Serbian policeman coming in, I really wanted to talk to them and to say that there was no reason for me to be a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have 23 minutes left, Mr. Seselj. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the 27th of February, 2008, you gave another statement to my associates, and in it you described that on that day, at 1550 hours, a Slovene woman violently entered your apartment, barged into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't write her name out here, but never mind. She came as a friend of the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, she came in a strange way. She did not announce over the telephone that she would be coming, or she didn't let us know in any other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, Your Honour, may we go into private session for a few moments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Personally, I don't see the need for this. I don't see what should be hidden. Witness, when the Trial Chamber was seized of all these issues, we appointed an amicus curiae, and the Trial Chamber made sure to find someone that was a professional, someone who was used to investigation, and that was the person that was appointed. This person was supposed to investigate, and we expected that when you met with this woman, you would give explanations on things. So she had a warrant by the Trial Chamber in order to investigate and to put questions to you to know exactly what happened. We are perfectly neutral. There are two parties here. There is the Prosecution, on the one hand, and the Defence, on the other hand. Both parties can allege what they want. But we have to judge, it is our responsibility, and because of this we have to double-check everything, which is why we had asked this woman to come and to investigate. She was on a mission, and she was there to tell you that given the Chamber's decision, she wanted to meet with you in order to put a number of questions to you. I wanted you to -- I wanted this to be very clear so you know exactly what the context was for all this. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Glamocanin, I would like you to describe to the Trial Chamber how it was that this lady barged into your apartment. So that I do not put leading questions to you, you explain it on your own?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This lady did not announce herself over the telephone or in any other way. Quite simply, she rang the doorbell of my apartment. I opened the door. She introduced herself, and she said straight away that she was looking for Jovan Glamocanin and that she had to talk to me. When I asked her who she was, she said that she was Ana Marhajn or something like that or something along those lines, and I said, "What is it we have to talk about? I don't know you." She said, "But we have to." I hesitated, but she entered the apartment. She didn't ask me -- she didn't wait for me to ask her to come in. She walked in and she said that she's Ana Marhajn, that she's a Slovene, and that she's a friend of The Hague Tribunal. When she said that, I threw her out of the apartment straight away, because if she was functioning on behalf of the OTP or some other organ of The Hague Tribunal, that was my reasoning, although there was little time for reasoning. She certainly would have announced herself. Why some kind of clandestine entry in this way, as if she were a commando or something. I had no other choice than to kick her out of my apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, but she said she was coming as an amicus curiae. I mean, you're an educated man. You must have understood that she was not a friend of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She did not say anything about Prosecutors. It's not that she mentioned a particular Prosecutor. But what kind of a friend of the Court is that? What does she have to discuss in that way? I would have accepted to talk to her, had she announced herself, had she explained. After all, Mr. Dan Saxon and Ms. Christine Dahl came to my apartment in a very civilised way. Why to barge in like a commando? I am not a criminal, I am not hiding anything. I am not involved in any kind of conflict. Why would anyone enter my apartment in that way? I know that one's apartment can be entered in accordance with the law and Constitution in agreement with me or with a search warrant from the Court; no other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your statement, it says that after this reaction of yours, she started threatening you too. She knew Serbian; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: She did speak the Serbian language, yes, truth to tell, with a Slovenian accept, but she said, "Wait and see until you get to The Hague."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So she started using two terms in the singular, which was the impolite form; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, impolite, and also it was a brief conversation and it was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you address her in "vu" terms all the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And she quarrelled, she started addressing you as "tu"?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, that's exactly what she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. In this statement dated the 11th of August this year, you mentioned this detail, too; namely, that you found it very strange to hear Stocchi and his colleague ask all these questions about the Serb Radical Party and about me, and that you thought that they wanted to represent the Serb Radical Party as some kind of a criminal organisation with a firm structure?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and with elements of violence in the party, considerable ones at that, and they asked me about all sorts of details that had nothing whatsoever to do with an investigation, the needs of the investigation, or the indictment. It went beyond that scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As you were upset, you cautioned them, warned them that this was improper behaviour, and you asked them whether they were perhaps from the American CIA, if they were putting questions like that. What was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, Paolo Stocchi said that he's not a member of the CIA. If he were to work for any intelligence service, he would work for his own Italian one, Italian intelligence service, and why, why be against the CIA? The CIA is the striking force of the West. Why not cooperate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On the basis of that, I draw the conclusion that for them, everything good is in the West and everything evil is in the East.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could we have a time frame for this particular discussion -- alleged discussion with the investigator that the witness is describing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell us when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was during those four days of interviews that were carried out in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was it in the first day, in the middle of these four days, at the end of the four days? Tell us when it occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, around the middle of the interviews. I think it was during the course of the second day of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They even suggested to you during this main interview that went on for four days that you, Maja Gojkovic and I had a meeting in Novi Zednik with the chief of police of Subotica, Milan Jerinkic, and that over there we agreed to compile a list of Croats who should be killed, who work for the Croatian Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right, that's what they discussed, and they wanted me to state my views. I said then and I can say now that I never took part in any such meeting, nor am I aware of the making of any such lists for liquidations in Subotica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On that occasion, Paolo Stocchi said to you, and now I'm quoting your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: "That Vojislav Seselj is dangerous for the new government in Serbia, that Vojislav Seselj is a hindrance and that Serbia should have a pro-Western government. Stocchi repeated several times that Vojislav Seselj is far worse than Slobodan Milosevic." Since I'm talking about Stocchi, I have to point out that during the course of these interviews, he said many things that were insults and slander, which I could not accept as a human being. He said that Vojislav Seselj is not a democrat, that he is unpleasant to his associates, that he slanders his political foes, and he asked for -- and he demanded from me that I confirm this in The Hague; is that right.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As for your qualification or, rather, what he said about you, it was in line with what Zoran Djindjic had told me and what I heard later during conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Later on, Saxon repeated what Stocchi had said, and I'm going to quote from your statement once again: "That Vojislav Seselj was a great danger, the greatest danger to the new government in Serbia, and the Saxon said that the concept of a Greater Serbia, advocated by Vojislav Seselj, was the war option, and that Vojislav Seselj was a danger to peace in the Balkans." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecution's team came to meet with you, and all they wanted to do was talk politics with you? They weren't there to investigate anything; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madame Lattanzi, we spent the first part of our interview discussing the topic war crimes and the indictment against Mr. Vojislav Seselj. I managed to convince Mr. Saxon that I knew nothing about any war crimes allegedly committed by Mr. Seselj, or hate speech, for that matter, either, and Mr. Saxon accepted that. Mr. Saxon is a very pleasant man. It's pleasant to talk to him. He has good manners. A good atmosphere prevailed during the interview, and I wanted to show him that I'm not an enemy to any people in the world, any nation, and that I was ready to talk and discuss matters, but that I could not be a Prosecution witness against Dr. Vojislav Seselj. And later on we went on to discuss politics, and he said, for example, that he represented American politics and that he was implementing American politics, and I even drew the conclusion that he was linked in a way to political life and might be some official of the American intelligence service. But when I put that to him, he laughed and said, "Well, why not?" And during that conversation, we also discussed politics, and he was a fervent advocate of American politics and policies. And let me state once again, that was my impression, and my basic conclusion, based on that interview with the Americans, is that they are all taken up with their politics, the politics of their government. It's a cowboy politics, but they see politics as the great rancher coming to another person's farm and says, "Give me your land or I'll kill your wife," and so on and so forth. But that's not the kind of relations that exist in the world. You have to respect other nations and other peoples. Other people have intellectuals, too. They have their own traditions, their own values. And what we can do is sit down to the negotiating table and reach agreements, and respect the civilizations, the legal systems, the European, Anglo-Saxon, and all the other civilizations and systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, your hearing went on -- your interview went on for four days. We know that, we have proof of this. It started in the morning, it went on in the afternoon, and it went on for four days. What about lunch? Did you have lunch with them or did everyone go and have lunch in different places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody had lunch. The talk went on all the time. Sometimes we spoke a bit more freely, and I got a bit passionate and emotional when I realised I was talking to a typical Italian, and I remembered all the stories of my mother, how an Italian officer grabbed me from the Ustashas when I was only one year old. It was in the native village of my mother, where we had fled from Banja Luka. That Italian officer had taken me away from a Croatian Ustasha who meant to spear me with a bayonet, so I have a great affection for Italians. And when I saw this Paolo Stocchi as a typical Italian, I sort of imagined him as a nephew of that Italian officer, but Paolo Stocchi was the one who led the conversation. He asked the questions. He led the conversation in a way that was convenient to him; that is, to incriminate, as much as possible, Dr. Vojislav Seselj, whereas I had no arguments, no motive, no grounds to incriminate Mr. Seselj, and I didn't give a statement of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you're an educated man, as I said earlier. You're a lawyer, and you are knowledgeable when it comes to procedure. Those 20 pages were supposed to sum up what you had said, so you really should have double-checked it in your own language, what this Mr. Stocchi had written, even if you found him very friendly, because he was drafting the statement from what you had said. And you should have controlled it, you should have double-checked it. Obviously, you didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not check it. He dictated, and on day 4 I described in which way I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had the impression that Mr. Seselj had indicated that he was reading from the February 2008 statement, when he described the similarities between the conversations had with the -- the alleged conversations had between the witness and Mr. Saxon, as well as Mr. Pastorre-Stocchi. I think I am mistaken -- I think Mr. Seselj was mistaken, so if he could please tell us where those quotes were coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 11th August, 2008, 11th of August. That's the last thing I quoted from. Maybe I was mistaken, I'm not sure, when I mentioned it the first time. Now, I still have some time left, don't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't have much time left, but you have 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The first time I read my statement, I have to be perfectly honest with you, Mr. Glamocanin, I was immediately suspicious it was really your statement, because there is some information here that is completely inaccurate. And I don't believe that even if you were very angry and very hateful, you would say a thing like that. You state here that it was clear to you that I had been in contact with Radmilo Bogdanovic, who during the war was the Minister of the Interior of Serbia. Radmilo Bogdanovic was Minister of the Interior until March 1991, and then after the protests of the 9th of March, he submitted his resignation. Did you remember I attended a press conference of the Serbian Radical Party, demanding his resignation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember you demanded his resignation, but you certainly did meet with Radmilo Bogdanovic, as had I. Radmilo Bogdanovic was a very talkative man and very witty, and he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to correct you here. As far as the Assembly is concerned, he was a vice-president of the chamber of republics and provinces, and there was another president of the upper house of the Parliament?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Radmilo Bogdanovic was a very pleasant man. Those were friendly meetings that do not impose any obligations on anyone, no political strings attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was incredible to me, when I read in the paragraph 120, that you allegedly stated that your son, Srdjan, had left the Serbian Radical Party and hated me because I was fighting only for power, and he wanted to fight against the Slobodan Milosevic regime. Do you know that my relationship with your son remained sincerely amicable even after you left the Serbian Radical Party, that he visited me both at the party, in my office in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that you wrote to him a very friendly letter, a very nice letter, and that he has only the greatest respect for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Glamocanin, when the Milosevic regime arrested me in 1994, you and I were in profound conflict, and your daughter came to attend a protest rally in my support?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it possible that you ever said anywhere that your son, Srdjan, hates me?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that he went to the front-line several times as a Serbian Radical Party volunteer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Twice, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And he commanded volunteers?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember he was in the group of volunteers that was surrounded in 1992 in Hrasno, in Sarajevo, somewhere in April, and they barely got out of a Muslim encirclement?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that publicly, an interview for the most popular paper in Serbia, I said that your son deserves to be a Chetnik vojvoda, but because his father is a high-ranking official of the party, we didn't want to give him that title?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it the 'Nedeljni Telegraf' for 1994? The Prosecution can find it. I see in paragraph 124 that they were very interested to locate the archives of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you see, they asked all sorts of questions outside the scope of their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that the Milosevic regime and the secret police, they put a lot of effort into finding our archives in the years when we were in a deep rift, but they never succeeded?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Milosevic regime used tried and tested police methods. They used the service of State Security that had been inherited from the Communist regime and that were to compromise all free-thinking and freedom-loving people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know that during that deep rift with them, I established within my party a group of people who would work on intelligence affairs and who would provide me with useful information on a daily basis? Do you remember Stojan?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I remember Stojan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You still don't know his real name, do you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't. You used to say that something like that was established, but I had never had anything to do with that sort of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that I have my personal archive as well, with several dozen thousand very confidential documents that nobody has ever been able to locate?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: You are a very meticulous man, a very thorough man, and you leave nothing to chance. You think always of the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They can't find it in my apartment or on the premises of the party. They can't find it anywhere. You know I also published several books, including those confidential documents, but always I was very selective. I never published the most interesting things. And I have three books of over 1.000 pages full of such documents.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know I was offered a lot of money from abroad to give those archives away, but I refused?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And many of these documents will remain inaccessible to the public, and I will take all these secrets to my grave. All right, Mr. Glamocanin. I was surprised by one more thing here, but you did explain in examination-in-chief; that it's something Stocchi imposed on you, as part of your statement, the bit that refers to Petar Panic; right? You know him well, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know him as your bodyguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was my bodyguard for three or four years. He accompanied me to the most forward front-lines?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But have you ever heard of him being involved in any sort of crime?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a rambunctious man, quarrelsome, a person who caused bar brawls, he was in prison several times but only because of these brawls and fist fights?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man who could be well liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But he was prone to fist fights. And how could they then confuse him with street dealers who traded foreign currency outside the building of our party?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN GLAMOCANIN (Resumed)
